children.translated_text: First Part

children.text: saudhe tuṅge saha dayitayā ko 'pi saṅkrīḍamānaḥ
children.translated_text: A certain supreme being, sporting with his beloved in a lofty palace,
fell asleep, as <s>Śrī</s> upon the coil of <s>Śeṣa</s>;
wondrous is this divine course of fate — in <s>Kāñcī</s>, adorned by the daughter of the mountain (<s>Śailajā</s>),
on the bank of the <s>Kampā</s> river, he awoke without her.
O handsome one, the dark-haired maidens brought you while you slept, playfully,
flying in celestial chariots from the city of <s>Varuṇa</s> to see the Lord;
even as they left you here, apprehensive at the command of the Goddess's attendant,
he then heard a disembodied voice in the sky thus:

children.text: kṣetre cāsmin sakalavipadāṃ bhañjane pañca māsān
children.translated_text: 'If you remain in this sacred place that destroys all misfortunes for five months,
the anguish of separation from your beloved will never befall you again.'

children.text: ākarṇyemāṃ punariti tathā saiṣa cakre nivāsaṃ
children.translated_text: Hearing this, he made his abode there accordingly;
even great hardship is praised if the outcome is laudable.
There, somehow crossing two or three months made exceedingly long by separation from his dear companion,
this one, tormented by desire — O <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Śiva</s>! —
at the onset of <s>Caitra</s>, delightful with the sidelong glances of the newly arisen beauty of spring,
beheld a cuckoo, relishing the taste of mango sprouts.
That [cuckoo], cooing with a melody sweet in the cadence of the fifth note —
overwhelmed by the memory of his beloved's speech, approaching it at a little distance,
offering an oblation of tears borne in the cupped palms of his eyes,
having gained some solace, he clearly dispatched a message in an audible voice:

children.text: atrāyāhi priyasakha nanu svāgataṃ paśya pārśve
children.translated_text: 'Come hither, dear friend! Welcome! Look beside you —
a mango creeper, sweating with drops of sweet sap that rise anew;
she certainly longs for union with you, O handsome one, all atremble,
with amorous bee-like eyes, beckoning with quivering sprouts, full of passion.'

children.text: antastoṣaṃ mama vitanuṣe hanta jāne bhavantaṃ
children.translated_text: 'You spread inner delight for me — ah, I know you
to be the foremost champion of the army of the five-arrowed king (<s>Kāma</s>);
under the pretext of cooing, offering beneficial counsel, O friend who uses the cuckoo as a pretext,
do you not unite proud women with their lovers?'

children.text: vācālaṃ mā parabhṛta kṛthā māṃ priyāviprayuktaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Do not make me talkative, O cuckoo — I who am separated from my beloved;
for words of love from those like me are generally addressed to ones like you;
and you, hiding somewhat in the cup of a sprout, O one of agitated soul with cuckoo-consorts,

children.text: tvaṃ cāpaśyan bata virahiṇāṃ yena jānāsi tāpam
children.translated_text: without seeing — alas! — how do you know the torment of those separated?'
'As long as my tongue recoils from commissioning you,
O honored lord of birds, to carry a message to my doe-eyed beloved,

children.text: tāvatkālaṃ tava ca hṛdayaṃ tāntimetīti śaṅke
children.translated_text: so long, I suspect, your heart too becomes weary,
being swift by nature yet made to be slow in arranging the appeal of this wretched supplicant.'

children.text: sandeśaṃ me naya khagapate sādhaya bhrātṛkṛtyaṃ
children.translated_text: 'Carry my message, O lord of birds! Fulfill a brother's duty!
O sweet-voiced one, console my beloved who is anguished by distress;
news of a lover, brought by a friend, for women tormented by separation,
generally becomes something that sustains their very life.'
'The land you must travel to, conquering the three worlds with auspiciousness at its fore,
has gained fame by the name of <s>Jayanta</s> of yore, of accomplished austerities,
beyond the <s>Cūrṇī</s> river, with <s>Govinda</s>'s chest as its neighboring expanse,
cooled by the nectar of <s>Lakṣmī</s>'s glances, in the land of <s>Kerala</s>.'
'There you shall behold this young woman, serving as a garland-crown for all women,
surely now dejected by my separation;
that auspicious one, with limbs tender as the stem of a golden plantain —
how could she endure the fire of <s>Kāma</s> (desire), blazing like a charcoal fire?'
'I shall instruct you on the route to travel without fatigue,
with cool shade from trees all around, the sun's heat allayed,
where, O lord of birds, having arrived, you shall surely adorn
those [trees], even the wild ones, with new and ever-new garden-pleasures.'
'The celestial ladies, having witnessed the festival called <s>Phālguna</s>
at the [temple of] <s>Śrī Kāmākṣī</s>, venerated by bowing gods, departing homeward in various celestial chariots —
their ears eager to hear your conversation — they shall be
your sweet-voiced companions all the way to the shore of the western ocean, to the city of <s>Varuṇa</s>.'
'Drawing in offerings of fragrance from ever-fresh creeper blossoms,
sprinkling the path all around with cool fine mist,
melodiously singing sweet-sweet songs with the humming of bees,
the breezes of the groves on the banks of the <s>Kampā</s> shall be your friendly and favorable companions.'
'Salute from a distance, dear friend, for the sake of seeing again,
this sacred temple of the Lord of <s>Kāñcī</s> (<s>Śauri</s>, i.e., <s>Viṣṇu</s>) on the elephant-hill slope,
which, with pigeons nesting in its golden pinnacle-turrets,
even today gives rise to the suspicion of smoke clinging from <s>Brahmā</s>'s sacrifice.'
'Among the eighteen seats, worship the honored <s>Kāmapīṭha</s>;
beyond the <s>Kampā</s>, the supreme Goddess herself is present here,
having obtained whose merciful rain — with the bow of her brow, the cloud of her eyes —
the land of <s>Tuṇḍīra</s> blazes with the abundant harvest of easily flowing poetry.'
'Flying up from this garden-grove fragrant with <s>bakula</s>,
proceed circumambulating to the sacred solitary mango tree in the precinct,
at whose root, O one naturally beautiful, renouncing longing for <s>Kailāsa</s>,
the Lord himself dwells — <s>Candracūḍa</s> (moon-crested <s>Śiva</s>), called <s>Valayāṅka</s>.'
'Having seen <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), as you quickly arise on the sky-path,
from the creepers fanned by the wind of your two wings,
young bees shall rise, their bodies drenched with nectar,
imitating the moist sidelong glances cast by the beauty of the garden.'
'As you, O cuckoo, clearly visible, grasp the edge of the sky,
the land of <s>Kāñcī</s>, adorning the earth with indescribable grandeur —
your heart captivated by its beauty, do not delay your journey;
for those like you, there is no greater object of esteem than the protection of a kinsman.'
'Taking refuge in the [southern] direction marked by the noose-weaponed one (<s>Yama</s>), moving with great speed,
its waves fanned by the chowrie-like fronds of areca palms blossoming on its banks,
you shall behold ahead the Milk Ocean (<s>Kṣīrasindhu</s>), fragrant with blooming lotuses,
attended by young bee-maidens intoxicated from drinking the honey.'
'With the splendor of your wings — deep blue like the ornamental line on the neck of the destroyer of cities (<s>Śiva</s>) —
pervading its expanse, with swaying trees bisecting the sky,
your path of flight above it shall clearly trace
the graceful line of a <s>Yamunā</s>-braid, born of love for the river.'

children.text: cūte cūte kusumakalikāṃ tvāṃ ca dṛṣṭvā sametaṃ
children.translated_text: 'At every mango tree, seeing a blossom-bud and you arrived together,
of slender women striking the young <s>aśoka</s> with their reddened feet,
with the delightful sounds of their anklets pleasing to the ear,
the garden-boundaries along the banks shall surely become vocal all around.'
'Women of <s>Dramiḍa</s> (Tamil) land, having bathed and emerged, with beautiful rounded breasts adorned with water-drops,
their bodies touched by dark fragrant unguents, wearing auspicious ornaments,
lovely to behold on the bank of that [river] —

children.text: prāyo bhāvī kṣaṇamiva sakhe gacchataste vilambaḥ
children.translated_text: upon seeing them, O friend, your delay shall probably seem but a moment.'
'With trees along the edges grayed by billows of smoke from oblation-fires,
the monasteries resounding with majestic and purifying <s>Brahma</s>-chants,
their expanses bounded by tanks purified by the bathing rites of the foremost <s>Brahmins</s> —
you should then see the <s>agrahāras</s> to the south of the river.'

children.text: sā vaidagdhī śrutiṣu sa punaḥ sarvaśāstrāvagāhas
children.translated_text: 'That erudition in the <s>śrutis</s> (Vedas), that mastery of all <s>śāstras</s> (sciences),
that unfading, flowing, flawless poetry —
of those who dwell there — what more need be said? — reciting all this,
parrots on every rooftop-tree shall make it manifest.'
'Passing beyond them, making fruitful the garland of eyelashes,
the upturned eyes of <s>Cola</s> women with necks raised smooth as smiling blue lotuses,
enter the <s>Bilva</s>-field (<s>Tiruvilvamala</s>), the abode of <s>Paśupati</s> (<s>Śiva</s>),
surely being summoned by the tips of flag-cloths on balconies fluttering in the breeze from the paddy-plains.'
'<s>Kāma</s> (the god of love), the master, attained the state of a moth in the sparks of [<s>Śiva</s>'s] eye —
"Fear not, fear not!" — by the sight of the moon-crested destroyer of mundane existence (<s>Śiva</s>);

children.text: śyāmā varṇe vacasi madhurā cañcalā dṛgvilāse
children.translated_text: dark in complexion, sweet in speech, restless in the play of her glances,

children.text: vāmotsaṅge lasati karuṇā kāpi kāmaṃ duhānā
children.translated_text: upon his left lap sits a certain compassionate one (<s>Pārvatī</s>), fulfilling desire abundantly.'
'With the loud, intoxicating songs of birds pronouncing words of welcome,
strewing flower-honey as an offering, fanning [you] with coral-sprouts,
the gardens there shall honor you, O friend, as the fragrant one's companion;
for people show equal affection to a king's friend as to the king himself.'
'At that time, courtesans with their loosening garments held in hand,
emerging from dense creeper-bowers after love-making,
free from perspiration by the breezes from your wing-rows as you sport about,
shall worship you with languid sidelong glances, weary with knitted brows.'

children.text: bhūyo gacchan janapadamimaṃ sa tvamullaṅghya colān
children.translated_text: 'Going further, passing beyond this <s>Cola</s> country,
you shall behold, tinged by the restless doe-eyes [of forest women],
forests with beds of blossoms, with scattered <s>guñjā</s>-berry garlands,
in bower after bower, the playful antics of <s>Śabara</s> couples being narrated.'
'There the breezes, spewing streams of pollen-spray from blossom-buds,
their course interrupted in the dense waterfall-spray,
delightful as they swing on the creeper-swings, caressable by the forest-goddesses,
shall attend upon you, bearing burdens of the tails of playful <s>camarī</s> deer.'
'Kissing the new sprout full of pollen as if kissing a <s>bimba</s>-fruit lip,

children.text: prāptāśleṣaḥ stana iva nave korake kāmacārī
children.translated_text: embracing the new bud as if [embracing] a breast, wandering at will,

children.text: bhoktāsi tvaṃ kamapi samayaṃ tatra mākandavallīḥ
children.translated_text: you shall enjoy for some time the mango creepers there;
when passion for a beloved is present and she is in bloom, what man is able to abandon [her]?'
'Having bitten with your beak the golden-brown blossom-clusters from the mango grove,
as you rise swiftly, the sky dappled by the shadow of your wings,
thinking you a fresh rain-cloud with lightning, playfully
the peacocks, dear friend, shall dance, their plume-burdens swaying.'
'Then, visible from afar, with royal swans alighting on its waves,
that <s>Kāverī</s>, a cascade of intoxicating waters from the elephant-<s>Sahya</s> mountain;
in the middle of which, dark as a cloud, reclining on the serpent, the jeweled rod of the earth,

children.text: madhye yasyā marataka iva prekṣyate raṅganāthaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Raṅganātha</s> is beheld like an emerald.'
'On its sacred banks, passing through <s>Hosala</s> settlements — cities, towns, and villages —
fragrant with the blossoms of garden-trees,
reach the abode of <s>Murāri</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), renowned as <s>Lakṣmīnārāyaṇapura</s>,
and become, O lord of cuckoos, the foremost among the holy.'
'Of the women dwelling there, with fragrant flowers placed in their beautiful tresses,
their bodices splitting on the slopes of breasts swelling with the warmth of youth,
their gentle smiles mingling with the rays of the pearl ornaments on their noses —
even <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love) himself becomes helpless before their charms.'
'If those beautiful women, their hearts knotted with pride, should not regard their bowing lovers,
O cuckoo, release just one <s>kuhū</s> call;
let there be, for the young men embraced by the vine-arms of their own trembling brides,
moist-smiling sidelong glances accompanying you.'
'You should take shelter on the <s>Sahya</s> mountain, renowned throughout the world
for the tinkling ornament-sounds of celestial women playing, making the creeper-bowers resonate,
on whose slope dwells the lord of the <s>Bhṛgu</s> clan (<s>Paraśurāma</s>), who voluntarily desisted from the destruction of the warrior class,
having made the entire circle of the earth into brahmins.'
'Seeing from afar the forest trees with rising smoke from forest-fires, their crests matted with flame-garlands,
buzzing with bees, brilliant with heaps of sprouts,
at once followed by warm and cool breezes,
in an ambiguous calamity, sudden reversal indeed produces anguish.'
'Having beheld <s>Śārṅgapāṇi</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>) in the <s>āmalaka</s>-land temple there,
descending from that mountain, folding your wings somewhat,
behold before you on the shore of the ocean the <s>Kerala</s> land, dense with areca palms,
flourishing — the enterprise of the arm-might of the son of <s>Bhṛgu</s> (<s>Paraśurāma</s>).'
'If you must pass by — enough! — the Lord <s>Candracūḍa</s> (moon-crested <s>Śiva</s>),
who dwells on the bank and who is wild from the destruction of <s>Dakṣa</s>'s sacrifice,
[near whom] stands <s>Bhadrakālī</s>, who with her three-pointed trident
slew the demon <s>Dāruka</s>, standing with the head of the lion-lord [at her side].'
'Sprinkled by the pure droplets of the waterfalls, worship him while standing in the sky;
stretching out, appearing as a dark new cloth covered with pearls —
if the attendants should chase you away, mistaking you for a crow,

children.text: kūjāṃ kiñcit kuru nanu girā vyajyate sannasaṃśca
children.translated_text: just coo a little — is not one's true nature revealed by one's voice?'
'Having thus worshipped the destroyer of cities (<s>Śiva</s>) with devotion and obtained his grace,

children.text: kṛṣṭaḥ kṛṣṭaḥ pathi pathi sakhe keralīnāṃ kaṭākṣaiḥ
children.translated_text: drawn again and again on every path, O friend, by the sidelong glances of <s>Kerala</s> women,
enter the capital of <s>Puralī</s> (the ruler of the land), whose lofty palaces
push the paths of the stars ever upward, and whose gardens are in full bloom.'
'In whose lineage was born the king named <s>Hariścandra</s>,
O bird, and [whose lineage is] the origin of the <s>Kaumārilas</s> and [their] doctrine of restitution;
in whose battles <s>Caṇḍikā</s> is present for the slaying of enemies —

children.text: teṣāmeṣāṃ stutiṣu na bhavet kasya vaktraṃ pavitram
children.translated_text: of these [rulers], whose mouth would not be purified in singing their praises?'
'With sidelong glances full of affection, saying "dear friend, [this is] the son,"
beheld by <s>Rukmiṇī</s>'s beloved (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>) as he abides in that city,
before him, in a young garden with blossoms freshly cut by tender women,
sporting somewhere, cast off the fatigue of the journey.'
'If a princess named <s>Svātī</s>, with anklets tinkling in play,
with tender feet, her hand resting in the palm of her companion, should come there
to worship the Lord — from her

children.text: svairālāpaistava pika girāṃ kāpi śikṣā bhavitrī
children.translated_text: your freely flowing conversations, O cuckoo, shall receive some instruction in speech.'
'Her coming — stooping and clinging under the weight of her breasts,
her face dotted with beads of perspiration, wearied by the burden of her hips —
sprinkle her a little with the load of pollen-spray held gently in your beak;
you shall receive from her the sidelong glances beautiful with fluttering eyelashes.'
'For some time, a blossom-cluster being enjoyed, its sprout-covering shaken off, trembling,
its young bees refused, when
you, O handsome one, are ready to depart — it would express its own grief,
releasing a few tear-drops with the pretext of dripping sweet nectar.'
'Although the direction you should travel is to the south, for the protection
of my very life, O friend, you should go westward again.'
The grove of <s>Dhūtārāma</s>, fanned by the breezes from the <s>Mukuṭa</s> river — there, of <s>Śambhu</s>,

children.text: sampadgrāmaṃ yadi na bhajase janmanā kiṃ bhṛtena
children.translated_text: the village of prosperity: if you do not worship it, what use is a life sustained?
With lofty mansions washed in white plaster, as if laughing at the silver mountain,
enter that magnificent abode of <s>Dhūrjaṭi</s> (Śiva), that treasure-house of splendor,
on either side experiencing the play of being a palm-leaf fan
for the earthly gods (Brahmins) wearied from their habitual prostrations.
Risen from the golden parapets where birds strut about undisturbed,
bow to the Lord of the Mountains with limbs held motionless in meditation, free of all fear;
"Is the reflection of his throat my husband?" — thus the Daughter of the Mountain
gazes upon you with curious, restrained, and sacred glances.
Beholding here and there with reverence the gods — <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Indra</s>, and the rest — whose mutual rivalry
is restrained by the frown of glorious <s>Nandī</s>, their service held in check,
and listening, O friend, in some places to the delicate
<s>vīṇā</s> melodies of singing <s>Kinnarī</s> women, indistinguishable from your own cooing.
You bestow divine sovereignty upon devotees, yet you live as a beggar;
you bear <s>Gaurī</s> on your lap, are smeared with ashes, and reduced <s>Pañcabāṇa</s> (the five-arrowed Love) to nothing;

children.text: kṛtsnaṃ vyāpya sphurasi bhuvanaṃ mṛgyase cāgamāntaiḥ
children.translated_text: pervading the entire universe you shine forth, yet are sought by the ends of the <s>Āgamas</s>;
who, O ocean of wonders, can truly fathom your essence?
Having praised thus, perch outside on the branch of a mango tree at the garden's edge;
remain there until the sun reaches the western mountain,
and you shall behold the <s>Tāṇḍava</s> dances of the moon-crested Lord, their fruit evident to the eye,
graced by the sidelong glances of <s>Girijā</s> delighting in her playful <s>Lāsya</s> dance.
At that hour, upon the circular tray held at the breast-terrace of the beautiful temple women
who bear great offerings — lovingly, as if upon the heart —
the splendor of the freshly risen moon with its clear markings enters, I suspect,
under the pretext of a <s>bimba</s> fruit, thinking 'this shall be mine.'
When the world is bereft of light, as if by clusters of radiance scattered from <s>Paśupati's</s> throat,
with darkness like black-lotus bees of the sky,
having rested somewhere upon the broad family of tree branches,
spend that night right there, with wings wearily drooping.
The shore breezes from the western ocean, rocking the waves,
having sipped nectar from water-lily buds drowsy with slight sleep upon the lakes,
stealing away the beads of perspiration born of lovemaking from beautiful women —

children.text: seviṣyante niśi parabhṛta tvāṃ sukhena prasuptam
children.translated_text: these shall attend upon you, O cuckoo, as you sleep blissfully in the night.
When dawn arrives, its first rays upon the mountain slope like a forest fire,
beautiful as clusters of young <s>Aśoka</s> blossoms in the sun's radiance,

children.text: prasthātuṃ tvaṃ punarapi sakhe prakramethāḥ prabhāte
children.translated_text: set forth again upon your journey in the morning, O friend,
for those like you find happiness in self-exertion for the sake of helping a friend.
Even as the beloved departs from a lotus's side and reaches the other bank,
beholding midway a <s>Cakravākī</s> bird overcome by the fever of <s>Māra</s> (love's anguish),

children.text: dūraṃ prāpte mayi vidhivaśāddūyamānāṃ sakhīṃ te
children.translated_text: remembering again and again your dear companion suffering by fate's decree with me gone far away,

children.text: smāraṃ smāraṃ dviguṇagamanotsāha eva dhruvaṃ syāḥ
children.translated_text: you shall surely feel your eagerness to travel doubled.
Having beheld <s>Bālakṛṣṇa</s>, the Lord dwelling in <s>Śambara</s> (Irinjalakkuda),
adorning the quarters of the sky marked by the friendship of <s>Lopāmudrā</s>,
proceed to where the fame of poet-kings like <s>Śaṅkara</s> and others, whose renown exceeds all bounds, spreads abroad,
through lands fragrant with <s>kola</s> berries, cardamom, and forest spices.
With mountain lords emerging again as if swiftly surfacing with wings,
plunged into by swarms of boats with arm-like oars flailing,
behold the ocean — the bed-chamber of <s>Lakṣmī's</s> lord, the flower garden of <s>Purāri</s> (Śiva),
the kitchen of all the <s>Maruts</s> (wind gods), the treasure-house of waters.
Its white sands strewn with nets of pearls scattered by garlands of waves,
clinging to the shore-path made lovely by flowering trees,
as you travel from land to land, sipped reverently
by the sidelong glances of doe-eyed women whose faces are raised with curiosity.
That renowned city called <s>Kukkuṭakroḍa</s> (Kozhikode/Calicut) shall delight your eyes,
whose palace towers scratch the sky,
which is protected by foremost heroes, lords of mountain and sea,
warrior chiefs whose arm-valor has made kings into sword-handles.
Where in every house stands a mansion washed with fresh white plaster,
on every mansion a pleasure-couch fashioned with fragrant flowers,
on every couch a pair of lover and beloved lost in passion,

children.text: yugme yugme sa khalu viharan viśvavīro manobhūḥ
children.translated_text: and in every pair, that universal hero <s>Manobhū</s> (Kāma, god of love) sports indeed.
Where a fresh blue lotus at the ear is superfluous when sidelong glances exist,
a pearl necklace is a burden on pitcher-like breasts when a radiant gentle smile shines,
and where, upon lustrous dark tresses of women whose eyes resemble young fawns,
when intoxicated bees are present drawn by the fragrance, flowers serve merely as auspicious ornament.
Where, I believe, the lord of rivers (the ocean), knowing that <s>Indirā</s> (Lakṣmī) has made her home in their own daughter (the city),
his heart agitated with affection,
repeatedly steals close with his waves, as if embracing,
the fleet of ships filled with heaps of gems gathered from hundreds of different island-lands.
On the rooftops of those mansions, you might begin to peck at the mass of radiance from red gems,
dense as vermillion, mistaking it for tender shoots;
seeing this, the young women with lotus-eyes placed at their lattice windows
would clap their hands over their quivering bosoms and laugh.

children.text: kṛṣṭvā dṛṣṭiṃ kathamapi tataḥ kautukānāṃ nidānād
children.translated_text: Somehow tearing your gaze away from there, driven by curiosity,
fly onward along the road, licking the flower-nectar of the trees,
stealing, stealing with your throat-songs — the war-drums of <s>Madana's</s> (Love's) army —
the hearts of longing women of the countryside whose eyes are like those of deer.
Reaching <s>Dīprā Prakāśa</s>, where conflicts are quelled by the practice of sacred learning,
proceed to <s>Śvetāraṇya</s> (Thrissur), the highly esteemed abode of the Conqueror of Death (<s>Mṛtyuñjaya</s>, Śiva),

children.text: dṛṣṭvā dūre sakṛdapi janā yanna paśyantyavaśyaṃ
children.translated_text: for those who have seen it even once from afar never again behold
the face of Death with its terrible frown knitted upon the brow.
The lotus foot of <s>Śambhu</s>, worthy of worship, which struck the chest of <s>Daṇḍapāṇi</s> (Yama),
fit to be massaged by the hands of the Mountain's Daughter,
when it was placed upon the Mountain Lord, he who regarded mountains as mere clods —
the emperor of <s>Rākṣasas</s> (Rāvaṇa), with arms crushed, cried out below.

children.text: pārśve yasya pravahati nilā nāma kallolinī sā
children.translated_text: Beside which flows that river named <s>Nīlā</s>,
fallen upon the head during the whirling of the twilight dance, like the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (Gaṅgā) herself,
on whose bank, lover of fertile fields and embraced by <s>Ramā</s> (Lakṣmī), there stands
a certain shrine dark as blue-lotus petals.
Where, in the beautiful gathering of <s>Kerala</s> women meeting with their lovers,
my beloved too, come for the great <s>Māgha</s> festival, O dear friend —

children.text: pāyaṃ pāyaṃ mukhaparimalaṃ mohanaṃ yatra mattāḥ
children.translated_text: drinking again and again the intoxicating fragrance of her mouth, the maddened
young bees even now mostly refuse to smell lotuses.
Her lotuses obscured by masses of moss, her geese upon the sandy banks departed,
the river, reduced to thinness by the sun's rays in these days,
her waist-zone of girdle-bells scattered with clusters of <s>āmalaka</s> fruits —
I think she, pitiable in the state of separation, follows my beloved.
If <s>Śāstā</s> (Ayyappa), who dwells in <s>Śambara</s> (the hills), her guardian,
should ride forth upon a swift horse along the riverside paths, eager for the hunt,
fan away his drops of perspiration with your gentle wing-breezes;

children.text: bhūyāt prītyai laghu ca samaye sevanaṃ hi prabhūṇām
children.translated_text: for service to the powerful at the right moment, however brief, brings great reward.
The Brahmin lords of <s>Kerala</s> are renowned as the most exalted in the world;
and among them, the greatness of the <s>Vallī</s> and <s>Kauṇya</s> families, especially those dwelling in the middle region, is beyond measure;
and wherever in that land these people of <s>Salilapavanā</s> (the Nīlā river region) are celebrated,
their virtues, learning, and influence surpass all others.

children.text: īṣṭe teṣāṃ stutiṣu na guruḥ kā kathālpīyasāṃ no
children.translated_text: Even <s>Guru</s> (<s>Bṛhaspati</s>) falters in praising them — what then to speak of lesser folk like us?
Brother, hear now the remainder of what was begun, in brief:
having crossed that river, amid groves of mango trees dripping with nectar,
alight upon those lands purified by the host of virtues of <s>Netranārāyaṇa</s>.
He who at the time of the wedding, by <s>Śambhu</s>, was compassionately
taken in hand and gently, slowly placed upon the stone surface —
that lotus foot, tender as a sprout, of <s>Kātyāyanī</s>, whose abode is <s>Muktipurī</s>,
the great battle-cry against the buffalo demon (<s>Mahiṣa</s>), must be seen.
A little before that, at the battlefield of <s>Raṇakhala</s>, pay your respects to the glorious one;
that is the sacred dwelling of the great sage, preceptor of both schools of <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>,
where, whenever assemblies of scholars arrive eager to debate,
flocks of parrots perching on the eaves of the lecture hall remain in attendance.
If exposition of the <s>Śāstras</s>, narration of <s>Harihara</s>, or pious hospitality to arriving guests,

children.text: ālāpo vā yadi saha budhairākṣipedasya cetaḥ
children.translated_text: or conversation with the learned should occupy his mind,
then, seated on a garden hillock surrounded by his trusted Brahmins,

children.text: kokūyethāḥ sa khalu madhurāṃ sūktimākarṇya tuṣyet
children.translated_text: let out your coo — hearing that sweet utterance, he would surely be delighted.
Appointed by me to a noble purpose, grounded in praiseworthy metrical form,
pleasing in its words, partaking of refined sensibility, of unerring conduct —
you, O friend, resembling a poem loosened somewhat by the long journey,

children.text: dhīmān paśyet sa yadi nanu te śuddha eva pracāraḥ
children.translated_text: if that wise man should examine you, your course is surely pure indeed.
Moving on from his side, carrying sacred fragrances,
the breezes white as <s>kunda</s> flowers, bearing the foam of cud from the mouths of the bull-lord (<s>Nandī</s>),
companions of <s>Vṛṣapurī</s> (the bull-city), marked by <s>Śaṅkara</s>,
scented with the fragrance wafting from the tossing tresses of playful <s>Gaurī</s>, shall cool your weariness.
If the front aspect, with eyes darting, is seen bowed under the weight of breasts,
the rear aspect, with graceful locks, the buttocked one, is not seen —
thus, the eight-formed Lord, desiring to behold both aspects of <s>Gaurī</s> simultaneously,

children.text: mūrtidvandvaṃ vahati bhagavān yaḥ sa muktyai niṣevyaḥ
children.translated_text: bears a twin form — He is to be worshipped for liberation.
When the forehead-eye blazes from the breath-winds of the serpent ornaments,
and drops of nectar flow copiously from the perspiring moon,
the circle of <s>Brahmā's</s> heads at His crown, within the hall,
dispels the doubts of earthly gods (Brahmins) who follow the path of the <s>Śruti</s>.
By the Guardians of the Quarters, stationed near the doorway, whose desires are fulfilled
by the sidelong grace of <s>Aṇimā</s> (the goddess), crowding the outer courtyard in devoted attendance —
entering nearby that golden temple out of devotion,

children.text: sampanmūrtiṃ praṇama girijāṃ sā hi viśvasya mātā
children.translated_text: bow to <s>Girijā</s>, the embodiment of prosperity, for she is the mother of the universe.
With the spreading slender radiance of the <s>Śauri</s> (Viṣṇu) of <s>Saṅgamagrāma</s>,
dark as <s>tamāla</s> blossoms, penetrating the expanse of sky,
enjoying the comfort of recalled new <s>tamāla</s> groves of matching hue,

children.text: manye lokaiḥ kṣaṇamiva pṛthaṅno vibhāviṣyase tvam
children.translated_text: I think the world will not distinguish you even for a moment.

children.text: kālīvāsaṃ bhaja pathi mahat kānanaṃ yatra śaśvat
children.translated_text: On the way, visit the great forest of <s>Kālīvāsa</s>, where perpetually,
when the host of gods arrives for worship, the sacrificial buffalo to be divided among the <s>Bhūtas</s> —
as fierce ones pull it by the horns, crying 'The great buffalo of offerings must be split!',
<s>Vijayā</s> (Durgā) restrains them with full-blown laughter as the rope is seized.
Behold ahead the lovely city of <s>Añjanakhala</s>, embraced by <s>Śaṅkara</s>,
with its charming mansion-flags and pennants fanned by the wind, yoked to the sun's rays,
where the powder-laden breeze, embraced by beautiful young women, kisses their perspiring cheeks
like a lover kissing the lotus-face of one weary from lovemaking.

children.text: sā ca prekṣyā saridanupadaṃ yatra kalmāṣitāyāṃ
children.translated_text: And that river too is worth beholding there, where in its waters stained
by the musk from the throats of women of the great festival-city bathing at the <s>Mahodaya</s> celebration,
the red lotuses, taking on the likeness of blue-lotus groves,
are clearly recognized when the great splendor of the dawn begins to unfold.
Beautifully clear, with fish for eyes, <s>Cakravāka</s> birds for the beauty of her breasts,
waves for eyebrows, lotuses for face, and lovely moss for hair —
she should be enjoyed, flowing sweet and willing, by those who descend favorably;
but for others she is unfathomable — such indeed is the way of the profound.
As you, O handsome one, hang playfully in the sky above the river,
seeing your reflection trembling in the water, flawless as a jewel's gleam,
thinking it a cluster of dark lotuses set in motion by the rush of waves,
the sweet southern breeze would coo and coo, O cuckoo, crying out to you.

children.text: tīraṃ tasyāḥ prati gatavato dakṣiṇaṃ tatkṣaṇaṃ te
children.translated_text: As you proceed toward the southern bank of that river, at that very moment
a land of all-surpassing splendor shall unfold before your gaze;

children.text: tāṃ jānīyā diśi diśi jayantākhyayā khyāyamānāṃ
children.translated_text: know that place, celebrated in every direction by the name <s>Jayanta</s>,
a realm that puts to shame the glory of the city of the gods.
With young gardens whose vine-bowers have been enjoyed by passionate women,
with lakes where pleasure-swans stir and bees wander bewildered through the city,
with gateway-towers whose pinnacles are set with rows of gems — that city
will likely be easy for you to recognize, O <s>Prajñābharaṇa</s>, even without being told.
<s>Uttarabhāga</s> (The Latter Part)
Filled with incomparable nets of gems, the birthplace and abode of <s>Lakṣmī</s>,
pregnant with mountains, praiseworthy in its growth from the rising of a portion of art,
regarding it as the supreme body of the ocean, vast —
there dwells <s>Rathāṅgī</s> (Viṣṇu's consort/Lakṣmī), that bee upon the Vedic lotus.

children.text: vaktraupamyaṃ vahati vimalaṃ paśya pārśve sudhāṃśoḥ
children.translated_text: "See, at the side of the moon, this bears the likeness of a spotless face;
O fair-faced one, look at the back" — thus addressed by their lovers,
the doe-eyed women in whose mansions, seeing this, cast a blemish upon the moon
with envious sidelong glances whose beauty rivals the blue lotus.
In every street paved with slabs of <s>Indra's</s> enemy (diamond/sapphire),
where, with spreading rays dark as the blue of your body's smoke,
when a darkness begins that even the sun's rays cannot dispel,
the amorous rendezvous of women with restless eyes proceeds fearlessly even in daylight.
Where at night, because the moon, its orb rubbed against the tips of mansion-pennants, commits
theft of the beauty of women's lotus-faces — truly —

children.text: dṛṣṭvā kṛṣṇaṃ kiṇamaṇikaṇaṃ hanta gāḍhaṃ prarūḍhaṃ
children.translated_text: seeing a dark jewel-like spot deeply grown upon it,
the foolish world says 'The moon has a mark' — but that is something else entirely.
Like garlands of young moss tossed up by the waves of the celestial river,
where the emerald-green rays emanate from the moon-chamber terraces,
the horses of the sun, stretching long across the sky-path like travelers,
mistaking them for grass, begin to chew with tossing muzzles.
Where in the garden, amid clusters of trees darkening the bower-thickets of the quarters
Clouds, indistinguishable from swarms of bees clinging to the peaks,
Release their waters, made even more fragrant, into the pools at the proper season,
Reflected again and again by the crystal rays at the tops of the stairways.
'Another woman ate at my gem-studded house before me!'—thus you accused, O innocent one, but your beloved [said], 'Is this mark of nails on the wall someone hiding?'
Thus in that [city], smiling slightly, the friends embarrass the newly-wed bride,
Showing her own incomparable form reflected [in the wall],
With a faint smile, they put the new bride to shame.
Upon the bow fashioned from the creeper of her eyebrows, a sugarcane shaft is fitted;
At the corner of her eye it carries the nature of an arrow, a lotus placed there;
Even in the line of hair on her belly, bearing the string of the bow of her <s>bimbā</s>-fruit lips,
Where the garland of bees has been dislodged by <s>Madana</s> (the god of love), the lord of the three worlds.
That [form], like a boat on the ocean of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment), with loosened braid, trembling breasts,

children.text: bhraśyannīvi sthitamiti viṭā vīkṣya saṃśliṣya yatra
children.translated_text: And slipping girdle—seeing it thus, the libertines, having embraced, where
The innocent wide-eyed women, with eyes half-closed, at the end of the tumult of enchantment,
Rouse again the effort of love-play, though weary once more.
Where the clouds, occupying the edges of the palaces of green emerald,

children.text: na jñāyeran śravaṇasubhagaṃ garjitaṃ cenna dadyuḥ
children.translated_text: Would not be recognized, if they did not give forth thunder pleasing to the ear;
And the streak of lightning, again engaged in newly begun love-play,
Is exactly like the swaying golden girdle slipping from the broad hips of a beloved woman.
In that [city], to the south, visible is the dwelling of the beloved of <s>Lakṣmī</s>,
The house of my beloved, surrounded on all sides by gem-studded halls,
Bearing in its midst a golden palace with overflowing clusters of rooftops,
In which <s>Śrī</s> (Prosperity) plays, as upon the shining pericarp of a lotus.
The great fortune—the display of the arms of the lord of <s>Rati</s> (Love)—from repetition,
A flood of auspiciousness—shines forth, for it contains the infinity of the connoisseurs, they say;
By the name formed from taking the first syllable of each of these [words],
The revered dwelling of <s>Mārakkaranilayam</s>, which the chief poets celebrate.
A playful bathing-pool sparkles there, lovely, on the stairway path,
Its clusters of lotuses ever smiling with the flashing of ruby rays,
Where, as my beloved comes to bathe in the clear water,
I think the jasmine-eyed fish dwell there to practice the art of her gait.
On its bank, again, is a garden, and there a young mango tree,
Surrounded by birds of your kind, O cuckoo, greedy for the taste of its sprouts;
And beside it, a charming <s>mādhavī</s> creeper, bent with clusters of blossoms—

children.text: preyasyā me pariṇayamahaṃ prāpitau sādaraṃ yau
children.translated_text: Those two, to whom my beloved and I lovingly performed a wedding ceremony.
Not far from that, on an emerald platform, with a basin bound in gold,
Watered at its root with loads of cool water, a certain <s>campaka</s> tree stands;
Having gained the friendship of your kind, that fortunate one, with the reddish glow of her smiling lotus-face,
Produces blossoms of a color matching her slender creeper-like body.
Free from the association of snakes, far removed in the dancing play of the household peacocks,
There is a grove of <s>pāṭīra</s> (sandalwood) trees, their dense shade stealing the sun's heat;

children.text: madhye tasyāṃ sa khalu latikāmaṇḍapo ratnabhūmiḥ
children.translated_text: In its midst is that very creeper-pavilion, with a floor of gems,
In which something of our vine of love always blossoms.
And near it, with its smooth trunk exuding sweet sap, somewhat,
A <s>kuravaka</s> tree, humming with bees, which for my doe-eyed beloved,
From time to time, with her arms swaying like elephant trunks,
Embraced in its limbs, bears under the guise of buds the goosebumps [she imparts].
If she is not seen seated upon a flower-bed prepared by her attendants,

children.text: adhyāsīnā parijanakṛtāṃ sā na cedīkṣitā syāt
children.translated_text: Eager, at any of these places I have described,
Then her most beloved palace of sapphire—

children.text: tasmin dṛśyā taṭidiva ghane cārurūpā priyā me
children.translated_text: There my beautiful beloved is to be seen, like lightning in a cloud.
She is a nectar-pill for the eyes, the essence of the Creator's creation,
The first bud of the moon of beauty, the lamp of Mother Earth,
The golden banner-staff of <s>Kandarpa</s> (Love), the lord of the three worlds,
The moon-digit of the ocean of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment)—my second life.
Seeing her immersed in the sphere of abundant loveliness,

children.text: madhye 'nyāsāmapi caladṛśāṃ jñāsyase no kathaṃ tvam
children.translated_text: How will you not recognize her even among other restless-eyed women?
When the world is bathed in a net of moonlight, near the stars,

children.text: cāndrī mūrtiḥ kathaya jagato jñāpyate kena rātrau
children.translated_text: Tell me, by whom at night is the lunar form not recognized?
A spotless moon of dense fragrance, dispelling darkness,
Two golden mountains, a portion of sky studded with swarms of bees,
A beautiful discus, a pair of soft elephant trunks, and a playful lotus—
All this, O gentle one, was assembled by <s>Madana</s> (Love), and she came into being.
Her languid, slow-rolling glances humble the deer;
Her brow, swaying with coquetry, takes away all the pride of the waves;
Her hands cannot bear the comparison with the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree;
Her voice bears an early friendship with the fifth note of your kind.

children.text: sā kāntiśceddravati kanakaṃ tanmukhaṃ cet ka induḥ
children.translated_text: If her luster flows, gold [loses its sheen]; if that face [shines], who then is the moon?
If the sweetness of her <s>bimba</s>-fruit lips [is tasted], honey turns bitter;

children.text: sā vā tasyā yadi tanulatā mālatī lohatulyā
children.translated_text: If her slender creeper-body [is seen], the <s>mallikā</s> jasmine is like iron;
If those thighs [are beheld], the golden plantain stalks are mere pretense.
As I speak again of these very limbs of hers, brimming with ever-fresh grace,

children.text: aṅgeṣvasyā mama kathayato hanta vācāṃ pravṛttiḥ
children.translated_text: Alas, the activity of my words goes on and on;

children.text: tādṛgbhūte manasi vivaśe kinnu kurvīta seyaṃ
children.translated_text: When the mind is in such a state, helpless, what indeed can it do?
Whatever the heart contemplates, that alone becomes the subject of speech.

children.text: adya prāyaḥ praṇayini mayi proṣite bhāgyadoṣāt
children.translated_text: Now perhaps, with me, her loving one, gone abroad due to the fault of fortune,
Longing through days that seem like <s>kalpas</s> (eons), alas,
She of delicate limbs, violently agitated by intense separation,
May have become like a weary peahen, overcome by the fever of burning heat.
Where, with the radiance of her sidelong glances as armor, pushing aside her hair slightly,
I placed with love a red lotus from the pond, day after day—
There, of her who is agitated with anxious thought, surely
Her hand-sprout rests on her cheek, an ornament beside her ear.

children.text: pakṣmaspandaḥ samajani sakhe paśyatormāṃ yayoḥ prāṅ
children.translated_text: Those eyes, O friend, whose lashes used to flutter when first seeing me,
But which fate has rendered leafless now that I am taken so far away—
Now those eyes of the doe-eyed one, restraining tears within,
Bear the pitifulness of lotuses rough with drops of dew.
That <s>bimba</s>-fruit lip of hers, which was once kissed by me with deep fragrance,

children.text: sambhogānte muhurapi mayā sādaraṃ cumbito yaḥ
children.translated_text: With passion, with remembrance, with yearning, tenderly, again and again at the end of love-play,
Being released by the sprinkling of the nectar of playful talk and traces of smiles—
Now languishes with the hot winds of her sighs.
Her two breasts, the twin play-mountains of the king of love, the pair of <s>cakravāka</s> birds of the flood of beauty,
Must surely be somewhat pale at their base,
My separation, making her cast off the necklace of pearls resembling the autumn moon,
I think, afraid, gives her instead another [necklace]—of streams of tears.

children.text: bhūṣāsvāsthāṃ yadapi jahatī tāṃ vahatyeva kāñcīṃ
children.translated_text: Though abandoning her usual care for ornaments, she still wears that girdle,

children.text: grāhaṃ grāhaṃ pṛthu pṛthu mayā mauktikaṃ gumbhitā yā
children.translated_text: Which was strung by me with large, large pearls, grasping them one by one;
With her great hip-sphere adorned by it, of her whose limbs are tender,

children.text: sālāvītāṃ sa kila madano manyate rājadhānīm
children.translated_text: They say <s>Madana</s> (Love) considers it a well-guarded royal capital.
Of her two thighs, which are the pair of tethering-posts for the elephant of my mind,
The pair, now sluggish from the weight of her hips, grows weary and weary;

children.text: ārabdhānāṃ hara hara mayā yatra saṃvāhanānāṃ
children.translated_text: Where, of the massages I had begun—alas, alas—
There always arose some interruptions, endless in their delight.
By the restless-eyed one, suspecting my arrival, from the door onwards,
Her lotus-feet, tender as sprouts, are wearied by her comings and goings;
Those very feet, by which false stumbling was often contrived—alas—
To obtain from me, during prostrations at her feet—alas—blows [of love].
Although the blazing fire of separation wastes her body-creeper,
It nevertheless doubles that beauty of grace;

children.text: taptāṃ taptāṃ nayati nitarāṃ tānavaṃ jātavedā
children.translated_text: The fire, making a golden streak thinner and thinner as it is heated more and more,
Nevertheless produces an even greater excellence of color.
Earth's dust in her tangled locks, a flood of tears in her eyes,
Her cheek resting on her hand, a net of white lotus-fiber necklaces on her breast-tips,

children.text: śroṇyāṃ kṣaumaṃ malinamasṛṇaṃ sā vahatyeva hantety
children.translated_text: A soiled, soft linen on her hips—she bears all this, alas!
But enough of this much lamentation—let there be no further waste of time!
Perching on the mango tree I first described, having bitten at will

children.text: daṣṭvā svairaṃ kisalayamatha prekṣaṇīyā tvayā sā
children.translated_text: A sprout resembling the lip of an innocent beloved, you should then look at her,
Whether she is asking about conditions in the <s>Malaya</s> mountains, or inquiring with modesty about my welfare,
Or entreating: 'Tell me news of the cruel one.'

children.text: chinte tāpaṃ himajalamayī cāndanī kinnu carcā
children.translated_text: 'Does a paste of sandalwood mixed with cool water dispel the fever?
Do the gently stirring breezes of the fans bring comfort?'—
When her companions of equal age thus ask, even as the burning grows excessive,
She may be smiling beautifully, reassuring her mind [saying] 'All is well.'
'The <s>Malaya</s> breezes are stirring—close the lattice with the shutters!
Frighten the five-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>) by invoking the name of <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), who shoots hosts of arrows!
Release the <s>jīvañjīva</s> bird to walk in the moonlight, O <s>Candrikā</s>!'
Thus she may be instructing her maidservant, with tearful eyes, again and again.
Or, supported by the hands of her attendants, reaching the painting gallery,

children.text: mugdhā svasyāścaraṇapatitaṃ veti taṃ māṃ nirīkṣya
children.translated_text: The innocent one, seeing me—that very me—fallen at her feet [in the painting], [may say]:—
'Come, rise up, dear one! I am not angry!'—with eyes brimming with tears,
Her hands trembling from a tight embrace, restrained by her friends.
'Abandon your anger, O fierce one! Fate alone has offended here,
By which, unexpectedly, this great separation of ours has come about'—
Thus, with hands joined, having imagined me angry before her,
She may be confidently offering, or preparing to conciliate [me] with a hundred sweet endearments.
Having seen her face reflected in the polished crystal wall—
Her face with disheveled, dust-grey locks hanging on her cheeks—
'Who has brought into the inner chamber this <s>Rohitāṅka</s> (the sun) veiled by fragments of clouds?'—

children.text: kenānītaḥ pura iti bhiyā vyāharantī sakhīrvā
children.translated_text: She may be exclaiming to her friends in fright.

children.text: nidrāṃ prāptā kathamapi cirāttatra cālokinī māṃ
children.translated_text: Having somehow attained sleep after a long time, seeing me there [in dream],
She may have contrived an empty embrace—alas, from the blow against her breast-mountains—
Breaking her bracelet held in her own hand, with only its remnant slipping off,
Or she may be binding [tears] in the lotus-eyes of her watching friends.
'A crow on the <s>kṣīra</s>-tree to the right announces the approach of a dear one;
My left eye has been twitching for a long time; today my heart revives;
Moreover, the song of cuckoos, pleasant to the ear, arises'—
Thus she may be somehow binding hope to her life-breaths, O brother.
She may be ashamed, thinking 'I give up! I am as good as dead!', or amazed,
Or hoping, 'The hope of his company is the supreme reason to live here again',
Or grieving over me, her beloved, who cannot endure separation—
In the activities of women arising from separation, this is but a mere indication.
Her left arm, which formerly used to be fanned for sleep

children.text: sambhogānte svapanavidhaye yaḥ purā dhūyate sma
children.translated_text: After love-play, aching from the knot of juice of the intertwining of tight embraces,
Drawn far from the embrace of my neck by hostile fate—
That arm of hers will tremble when you are near.

children.text: vakturvaktraṃ tamasi bhavato naiva dṛśyeta rātrāv
children.translated_text: At night, in darkness, the face of the speaker—yours—would not be visible;
Until midday, she is occupied with her daily observances;
When the sun's rays become bearable to touch, her unbearable pangs of love—
Standing on the gem-studded balcony, you should convey my message to her.
'Having left even the blossoming mango trees, this one has come to my presence—
Who could this be, wishing to announce some message of good tidings?'
Thus, as her friends wipe her eyes with a hand bearing drops of water,
Having been seen, you should begin to speak slowly, in clear syllables.
'Your auspicious ornament of beauty is unfading, O woman of lovely limbs!
I have come from the side of your husband, a friend, bearing a message.

children.text: jātaṃ viddhi śrutisukhagirāṃ kokilānāṃ kule māṃ
children.translated_text: Know me to be born in the family of cuckoos, whose songs are sweet to the ear—
We who are the sixth weapon of the five-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>), somehow drawing travelers [with longing].'

children.text: coleṣvāste sumukhi kuśalī tvatpriyaḥ pṛcchati tvāṃ
children.translated_text: 'Your beloved dwells in good health in the <s>Cola</s> country, O beautiful-faced one, and asks after you—
"Does well-being attend you?"'—Having thus begun to speak,
'Tell me more! Tell me more!'—she will repeatedly implore, and with
Sidelong glances mixed with tears and smiles of joy, the intoxicating-eyed one will honor you.

children.text: evaṃ brūyāḥ punarajani yaḥ premakope mitho vāṃ
children.translated_text: Then you should say: 'Once, when a lover's quarrel arose between you two,
When silence fell, he, quick and impetuous, was the first to speak;
This is the speech of that lord of your life, separated for so long, of such love—
Hear it from me, sweet to the ear, beautiful in its composition.'
'O woman of auspicious limbs! With my outer senses, which fail to find you, my dear companion,
I reach some indescribable state;
But this blessed heart, day and night, heedless of everything else,
Is immersed in you—alas, how different are the fortunes even of those born together!'
'Tossing in the pool called anguish, threatened by the terrible

children.text: ātaṅkākhye sarasi luṭhato hā niśīthe niśīthe
children.translated_text: Breezes of white lotuses and maddened bees, alas, in the depths of night, in the depths of night,
When the world is mute with sleep and I weep, consumed by sighs and anxious thought,
The wailing <s>cakravāka</s> birds are my companions, O you of darting eyes!'
'Delusion reigns supreme, fortitude dissolves, drowsiness enters,

children.text: bhātyunmādo bhramati matirityādi so 'haṃ na vedmi
children.translated_text: Madness shines forth, the mind wanders'—thus and more, I do not know;

children.text: bāṇaṃ muñcan parisaracaro na svapan nāpi khādan
children.translated_text: Not sleeping, not eating, wandering about releasing arrows—
Only the five-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>), O woman of languid gait, knows all this.
'At this very season, the lovely creepers, their fresh sprouts trembling,

children.text: kamrā vallyaḥ kimapi marutā cumbitā dakṣiṇena
children.translated_text: Bearing golden blossoms, kissed somehow by the southern breeze,
Remind me of you, O beloved, at the time of our love-play in the past—
You who were slightly biting your sprout-like lip, hissing softly, waving your palm.'
'That gentle breeze, companion of the fragrance of blooming <s>bakula</s> flowers,
Which used to wander charmingly near the gem-latticed windows of yours

children.text: smāraṃ smāraṃ kathamapi mayā muhyatā sahyate 'sau
children.translated_text: After our play in the past, with your hair-mass loosened, hanging over your shoulders, the edge of your garment held back by your hand—
Remembering and remembering that, I, swooning, somehow endure it, O slender one.'
Having somehow crossed the great night of separation with intense suffering,
Seeing the reddish ray of the sun at the horizon of <s>Indra</s>'s quarter,
The delicate lady rushing forward to meet [it], clinging as if to the boundary of fortune —
My mind yearns, alas, O doe-eyed one, for the young one named <s>cakra</s> [the <s>cakravāka</s> bird reunited with its mate at dawn].
I am filled with longing; at the sound of the charming female goose, my thoughts turn to you;
Upon your ornaments that steal my heart, I constantly cast my eyes;

children.text: tvatsaṃspṛṣṭe mama ca vapuṣi prema badhnāmi kānte
children.translated_text: And upon my body that was touched by you, I fix my love, O beloved;
Truly, I sustain even my very life-breaths only because they are dear to you.
'You and I have both come to the same earth' — this thought of non-separation,
'Remember, you with your reproaches!' — the pleasure of mutual exchange of words,
Our bodies are touched simultaneously by moonbeams at night —
By that too, O one who walks like an elephant, there is truly a sense of embrace.
Alas, in this separation where mutual seeing is not easily obtained,
That same blessed creeper of meditative imagination is my sole support;
Seated, having embraced you tightly many times through that [meditation] out of passion,
Placed upon my lap, O one with heavy hips — it is not fitting to say more.
My heart has now become a fit target for the warrior <s>Madana</s> (the god of love),
With many wounds; surely from that, O beautiful-browed one, my steadfastness has fallen;

children.text: kālāt kṣīṇe punaravayave vardhate kevalaṃ no
children.translated_text: Though my limbs are wasted with time, all that grows is
The heat — from the fierce fire of <s>Smara</s> (Love) — and even the rising of its color [the reddening of the body from love's fire].

children.text: evaṃprāyā na hi na virahe jīvituṃ santyupāyāḥ
children.translated_text: For indeed, there are such means of staying alive in separation;
Truly, having sustained my steadfastness through these various means, I live on, O lord of my life;
Having resolved thus, O one of incomparable virtues, I have turned away from rash acts;

children.text: tvaṃ ca snānādiṣu savayasāṃ prārthanāṃ mā niṣedhīḥ
children.translated_text: And do not refuse the invitations of your friends for bathing and the like.
The ocean of separation is mostly crossed, by the grace of <s>Śailakanyā</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>, the mountain's daughter);
The remaining two months, O delicate one, should be endured — do not despair;
Then, O timid one, in the palace chambers fragrant with incense vapors,
We shall sport during the days resounding with the deep rumbling of fresh rain-clouds.
Does there ever flash in your mind, O restless-glanced one, that memory of the bathing-powder chamber —
Your face with its fallen flower-ornament, whitened eyes, and washed <s>bimba</s>-fruit-red lips,

children.text: snānānte te mukhamupasakhi prekṣamāṇe mayi drāg
children.translated_text: That face of yours after bathing, as I quickly gazed upon it, O friend,
And that plunging of us both again into water up to the chest?
Having seen there in the pleasure garden a certain young mango tree
Embracing many creepers with its branch-arms,
With your face turned sideways, lips quivering, O fierce one,
A sidelong glance was sent at me, with beautiful brow-furrowing, glistening with tear-drops.

children.text: pratyākhyātaḥ praṇayini ruṣā bimbito 'haṃ stane te
children.translated_text: Rejected by you in love out of anger, my image reflected on your breast,
The maidservant, unknowing, began to cover it with sandalwood paste;

children.text: mā pāṭīraṃ pulakini punaścātra limpeti śaṃsaty
children.translated_text: 'Do not smear sandal paste there again!' — so you declared, O one with goosebumps;
As the group of girlfriends smiled, you cast a glance full of bashfulness.
As you were gathering garden flowers with your hand, beautiful as a young shoot,
Bees, greedy for the fragrance of your lotus-face, together with me,
Your playful companions, as if frightened by the pollen of the flowers,
For some time covered their eyes with their tender-shoot-like hands.
From this, know my well-being through the gift of this recognition;
And furthermore, hear one more thing — the persuasion of a companion through tender insistence:
When the playful goose, seized by love, forcibly kissed [its mate, and she] exclaimed,

children.text: tvaṃ tu smṛtvā kimapi bahalavrīlamālokathā mām
children.translated_text: You, remembering something, looked at me with intense bashfulness.
'Love is said to break by separation' — so goes the common saying;
But my love, connected to you, is a hundredfold greater in separation than in union;

children.text: so 'yaṃ bhedo viṣayabhidayā saṅgame tvaṃ kilaikā
children.translated_text: This is the difference, caused by the distinction of objects: in union, you are but one;

children.text: viśleṣe tu tribhuvanamidaṃ jāyate tvanmayaṃ hi
children.translated_text: But in separation, this entire three-world becomes pervaded by you.
Having done this task, dear friend, for me, your brother in distress,
You would not be without reward in the world's share among the compassionate;

children.text: śaṃsanti tvāṃ nanu parabhṛtaṃ śaiśave yadbhṛto 'nyaiḥ
children.translated_text: They call you <s>parabhṛta</s> (one raised by others), since you were raised by others in childhood;
Now you, the ornament of the winged ones, through your nurturing you yourself support others.
Having thus sustained her life, distressed by separation,
Go, roaming at your will, to whichever direction you desire;
May the venerable glory of <s>Madana</s> (Love), the king, be favorable to you, O cuckoo;
May there never again be even a single occasion of separation from her.
